items.stem: Where should an OpenAI API key be used so it is not exposed to end users?

options.text: On a server-side component, never in client-side browser code
options.rationale: Correct: keys must stay server-side; client-side code is visible to users.

options.text: Hard-coded in the front-end JavaScript bundle
options.rationale: Front-end code is downloadable, exposing the key to everyone.

options.text: In a public GitHub repository for convenience
options.rationale: Publishing a key leaks it immediately.

options.text: In a URL query string to every browser
options.rationale: Keys in URLs are logged and exposed; this is insecure.

items.explanation: Correct: keys must stay server-side; client-side code is visible to users.

items.stem: An API call returns HTTP 429. What does this indicate and what is the right response?

options.text: A rate/quota limit was hit; back off and retry later
options.rationale: Correct: 429 signals too many requests; the client should back off and retry.

options.text: The key is invalid and must be regenerated

options.rationale: A missing model is a different error, typically 404.

items.explanation: Correct: 429 signals too many requests; the client should back off and retry.

items.stem: Which TWO practices keep API keys secure in a deployed app? (Select TWO)

options.text: Store keys in a secret manager or environment variable, not in code
options.rationale: Correct: secrets belong outside source code and client bundles.

options.text: Rotate keys periodically and on suspected exposure
options.rationale: Correct: rotation limits the window a leaked key is useful.

options.text: Embed the key in client-side JavaScript
options.rationale: Client-side code exposes the key to all users.

options.text: Email the key to the whole team in plain text
options.rationale: Sharing keys in plaintext spreads and risks the secret.

items.explanation: Correct: secrets belong outside source code and client bundles.
